title: NRT vs TypeScript strictNullChecks (compile-time only)
hook: Both C# nullable reference types and TypeScript strictNullChecks are compile-time stories. Neither stops null from arriving at run time from JSON, Redis, or a missing SQS attribute.

blocks.text: If you know TypeScript’s `strictNullChecks`, you already understand the *shape* of C# **nullable reference types (NRT)**: annotate types, let flow analysis warn, use optional chaining and nullish coalescing, and treat `!` as an escape hatch. The differences matter in interviews: C# has **`Nullable<T>`** as a real struct for value types, one `null` instead of JavaScript’s `null` and `undefined`, and **NullReferenceException** as a distinct runtime failure from TypeScript’s **TypeError**.

entries.plainDefinition: Compiler option that makes null and undefined part of the type system. Closest TypeScript analogue to C# NRT.
TypeScript removes type annotations when emitting JavaScript. C# keeps metadata but NRT annotations do not change reference-type layout.
entries.example: `string?` and `string` are the same CLR type at run time.

entries.plainDefinition: Runtime exception when you dereference a null reference in C#.
JSON, Redis strings, and message queue bodies arrive without compile-time types until you validate.
entries.example: `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>()` can return null or partial objects.

blocks.text: Mixed-stack teams often overclaim: “C# 8 made null impossible” or “TypeScript is safer because it has undefined.” Both are wrong. A green build in either language is not proof that Redis returned a session or that JSON contained every non-nullable property. Design validation at boundaries in both ecosystems.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: “strictNullChecks and NRT are cousins — both compile-time, both optional historically, both on by default in new templates. C# additionally has `Nullable<T>` as a CLR type and real NullReferenceException at run time.”

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: Same compile-time contract, same runtime gap

items.title: Annotate intent
items.body: C#: `string` vs `string?`. TS: `string` vs `string | null` (and often `| undefined`).

items.title: Flow analysis warns
items.body: Both narrow after checks. C# uses attributes for Try* patterns; TS uses type guards and assertion functions.

items.title: Run time still untyped at edges
items.body: Deserialize, parse, and network I/O bypass the checker unless you validate explicitly.

diagram.title: Compile-time vs run-time null
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph C# [C#]
    NRT[NRT warnings] --> CLR[CLR still has null refs]
    NV[Nullable T struct] --> CLR
  end
  subgraph TS [TypeScript]
    SNC[strictNullChecks] --> JS[JS null and undefined remain]
  end
  WIRE[JSON / Redis / SQS] --> CLR
  WIRE --> JS

snippet.label: Same lie, two compilers — deserialize boundary
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `!` suppresses the compiler; run time can still be null or missing fields. Lines 4–5: TS `as` assertion is the same class of trust — validate before trusting nested properties.

snippet.label: Value type null exists only in C#
snippet.explanation: Line 1: C# value-type null is a struct with HasValue. Lines 4–5: explicit test and coalesce. TypeScript has no built-in nullable struct — only union types erased at emit.

snippet.label: Shared mitigation — optional chaining
snippet.explanation: Line 1: C# `?.` and `??` mirror JS/TS optional chaining and nullish coalescing. Both short-circuit on null; neither validates that the wire format matched your DTO.

blocks.title: Side-by-side null models
rows: JS has both null and undefined

blocks.title: Claiming C# 8 made null impossible
blocks.body: NRT added warnings, not runtime enforcement on references. Reflection, deserialization, and cache misses still produce null.

blocks.title: Equating undefined with int?
blocks.body: TypeScript undefined is a JavaScript value. C# `int?` is a struct with HasValue. Different machines — do not conflate them in cross-language design.

interviewTakeaways: NRT and strictNullChecks: compiler warnings, no runtime rewrite of reference types.
C# still has `Nullable<T>` and NRE; TypeScript still has null, undefined, and TypeError.
Wire formats (JSON, Redis strings, SQS bodies) are untyped until you validate.
commonPitfalls: Saying ‘C# 8 made null impossible.’ It made warnings possible.
Trusting `Deserialize<T>()` or `as T` because DTO properties are non-nullable in source.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Closest analogue to `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`. Both vanish at emit; both use `!` as an escape hatch.
`obj.foo` when obj is null is TypeError in JavaScript and NullReferenceException in C#. Optional chaining is the shared mitigation.
